newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate Leader Lott says no budget progress.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate Leader Lott says no budget progress.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said on Monday the White House and Republicans had made no progress on a balanced budget pact, forcing lawmakers to begin work on their own budget plan.

"No progress has been made. The president has not been willing to address some of the issues that are controversial," Lott told a news conference. "We're also going to begin working on the next plan and that would be to come up with a congressional plan."
Lott said he would like to work with Democrats. He said Republicans were committed to a tax cut in any budget pact.

Republicans had hoped to use President Clinton's five-year budget plan as the basis for a budget deal. In the wake of recent Congressional Budget Office estimates that the plan will be $69 billion short of balance in 2002, Republicans have asked the White House to send up a new budget.

Lott said he was also disappointed that Clinton did not take him up on his call for a bipartisan commission to see whether the Consumer Price Index overstates inflation. Because many entitlement program increases are based on the CPI, adjusting it could produce major savings toward a budget deal.
Lott said he wanted a major tax cut in any budget deal. Republicans have recommended nearly $200 billion in tax cuts over five years, about twice the level Clinton has requested.
To pay for the tax cut, Republicans might have to seek deeper cuts in entitlement spending than Clinton's budget.

Asked if Republicans would have to back off their tax plan Lott said, "That's not what I would prefer to do. It's important we have tax fairness. I think it's important we have some incentives for growth in the economcy."
But he added Republicans had to approach the budget with nothing off the table.

Lott said Republicans hoped to work with conservative Democrats on any budget. He said that after defeating a balanced budget amendement to the constitution, Democrats had an obligation to help craft a budget plan.
"The Democrats said we don't need a constitutional amendment for a balanced budget. They said we need a balanced budget. Now what are they going to say? We don't need a balanced budget?" Lott said.
The Senate failed by one vote last week earlier this month to muster the two-thirds majority needed to approve a balanced budget amendment, after a key Democrat decided to vote no.
